title: How Design Software Handles Team Collaboration
description: An analysis of real-time collaboration features across Figma, Sketch, Framer, and InVision — covering multiplayer editing, review workflows, comment systems, and cross-functional handoff for design teams.
body:
Design collaboration has shifted from a feature checkbox to a primary selection criterion. The question is no longer whether a design tool supports comments — it is how smoothly a team of designers, product managers, engineers, and stakeholders can work together across time zones without creating version conflicts, lost feedback, or misaligned expectations.

This analysis examines how four design tools handle the collaboration dimensions that matter most to real teams: simultaneous editing, review and approval workflows, comment resolution, and cross-functional access.

## Simultaneous Editing

Figma's multiplayer editing is the benchmark against which other tools are measured. Multiple designers work on the same file simultaneously, with each person's cursor, selection, and edits visible in real-time. The system handles conflict resolution automatically — when two designers modify the same property, the last write wins, and all participants see the update within seconds. Figma's multiplayer extends to prototyping mode, where team members can simultaneously test interactive flows and discuss behavior in real-time.

The practical impact of Figma's multiplayer is that design reviews happen on the live file rather than on exported screenshots. A design lead can watch a junior designer build a component, suggest changes in real-time, and see those changes applied immediately. This eliminates the review cycle of export-comment-revise-export that consumes hours in asynchronous workflows.

Sketch's collaboration model evolved from single-user desktop files to cloud-based team projects. Sketch for Teams allows multiple designers to work on files within the same project, but simultaneous editing of the same file is limited. Designers typically work on separate files and merge changes through Sketch's version history. The collaboration model works for small teams where designers own distinct areas of the product but creates friction for larger teams that need real-time co-editing.

Framer supports multiplayer editing for pages and components, with real-time cursors and selection indicators. The collaboration model is similar to Figma but scoped to web pages. For teams building marketing sites, Framer's collaboration allows a designer to work on page layout while a content writer edits copy in the same file. The limitation is that Framer's collaboration does not extend to the level of component-level simultaneous editing that Figma provides.

InVision does not support simultaneous design editing. Its collaboration model is built around asynchronous review: designers upload completed screens, and reviewers leave comments on specific frames. The absence of real-time co-editing means InVision functions as a review and feedback tool rather than a design collaboration platform.

## Review and Approval Workflows

Figma's review workflow integrates comments directly into the design canvas. Reviewers select an element or frame, leave a comment, and the comment anchors to that specific design element. Comments support threads, mentions, emoji reactions, and resolution status. Resolved comments are archived but remain accessible, creating an audit trail of design decisions.

Figma's approval system uses file-level status indicators: designs can be marked as In Review, Approved, or needs Revision. Combined with branching and merging, this creates a lightweight approval workflow where design changes are proposed on a branch, reviewed through comments, and merged into the main file when approved.

Sketch's review workflow depends on Sketch Cloud, where designers publish files for stakeholder review. Reviewers access designs through a web browser, leaving comments on specific frames. The comment system supports threads and resolution, but lacks the element-level anchoring that Figma provides — comments attach to frames rather than specific design elements, which can create ambiguity about which component a comment references.

Framer's review workflow uses its built-in commenting system, where reviewers leave comments on published pages. Comments anchor to specific elements and support threading. For marketing teams, Framer's review workflow integrates with the publishing pipeline — comments on a draft page can be addressed before the page goes live, creating a built-in approval gate.

InVision's review workflow is its core product strength. The platform was built specifically for design review, and its commenting system reflects that focus. Reviewers leave time-stamped comments that anchor to specific screen regions, and designers track comment status through a resolution workflow. InVision's Boards feature allows teams to organize designs into review collections, vote on alternatives, and track approval status across multiple design options. For teams where design review is the primary bottleneck, InVision's workflow remains purpose-built for that problem.

## Cross-Functional Access

Figma's cross-functional access model is built on role-based permissions and shareable links. Designers, developers, product managers, and external stakeholders can access the same design file with appropriate permission levels. Developers use Dev Mode for inspection, PMs use the standard viewer for design review, and external stakeholders use comment-only links for feedback. The shared workspace eliminates the file-sharing overhead that historically separated design from other functions.

Sketch's cross-functional access requires Sketch Cloud or Sketch for Teams. Non-designers access designs through a web viewer that supports comments and basic inspection. The access model is more limited than Figma's — developers cannot inspect CSS properties or component specifications through Sketch's native viewer, requiring third-party tools like Zeplin for developer handoff.

Framer's cross-functional access is built into its publishing model. Designers publish pages to a staging URL where team members review, comment, and test interactive behavior. The published prototype runs in a browser, requiring no special software for reviewers. For teams that deploy Framer prototypes to production, the review URL is the same as the production URL, eliminating the gap between what was reviewed and what shipped.

InVision's cross-functional access centers on its review interface. Reviewers receive a link to a screen collection, view designs in a browser, and leave comments without needing any design software. The simplicity of InVision's review interface makes it accessible to non-technical stakeholders who may find Figma's full design interface overwhelming.

## Asynchronous Collaboration Across Time Zones

Figma supports asynchronous collaboration through its comment system, version history, and branch-based workflows. Designers in different time zones work on separate branches, leave contextual comments explaining their decisions, and merge changes when team members in other time zones review. Figma's notification system alerts team members to new comments, branch updates, and file changes, keeping asynchronous workflows visible.

Sketch's asynchronous collaboration relies on Sketch Cloud file sharing and version history. Designers publish updates to Sketch Cloud, and team members review changes through the web viewer. The absence of real-time co-editing means Sketch's asynchronous workflow is its only collaboration mode, which works well for teams accustomed to file-based workflows.

Framer's asynchronous collaboration uses its publishing and commenting system. Designers publish updated pages, and team members review changes at their convenience. The page-based publishing model means asynchronous reviews focus on complete pages rather than individual components, which aligns with how marketing teams evaluate design work.

InVision's asynchronous model is its native workflow. The entire platform is designed for team members to review designs and leave feedback on their own schedule. For globally distributed teams where synchronous collaboration is impractical, InVision's asynchronous review workflow remains a practical choice.

## Choosing Based on Collaboration Needs

Figma serves teams that need real-time collaborative design with integrated review, developer handoff, and cross-functional access in a single platform. Sketch serves small Mac-native teams that work synchronously and use external tools for handoff. Framer serves marketing and product teams where collaboration centers on publishing and reviewing complete pages. InVision serves teams where asynchronous design review and stakeholder feedback are the primary workflow requirements.

The collaboration capabilities of design tools increasingly determine team productivity. A tool with excellent design features but poor collaboration creates bottlenecks that slow the entire product development process, while a tool with strong collaboration capabilities compensates for design limitations through faster feedback loops and reduced miscommunication.
